newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian voters desert ruling Socialists.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian voters desert ruling Socialists.

text.p: Bulgarian voters have shown their anger at years of economic hardship by dealing a heavy blow to the governing Socialists in the first round of presidential elections.

Unofficial projections based on early results from Sunday's vote showed opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov had comfortably beaten the Socialist Ivan Marazov into second place but had failed to win an absolute majority.
"I have to admit that a lot of people voted against us because they were disappointed in the policies of the Socialist government," Marazov, who polled less than 30 percent, told reporters.

Projections from independent polling groups put Stoyanov's vote at between 43 and 44 percent, with flamboyant former emigre George Ganchev, whose Bulgarian Business Bloc is a virtual one-man show, just three or four points behind Marazov.

Stoyanov, candidate of the Union of Democratic Forces, hailed the vote as a sea-change in voting patterns among Bulgaria's 6.75 million electorate and predicted he would win the second round on November 3.
"The vote shows that a new majority is being formed," Stoyanov told a news conference. "Half of it supported the new and reasonable programme represented by me."
The other half, he said, had "chosen the path of complete negativity" by voting for Ganchev. "I expect them to vote for me in the second round," Stoyanov added.

Ganchev's small party usually votes with the Socialists in parliament and Socialist spokesman Georgi Parvanov said he expected the leftist vote to consolidate in the second round, but Ganchev insisted his party was independent and ruled out any deal.
"I will not appeal to my electorate to vote for another candidate if I cannot continue," he said.
The electoral committee put turnout at some 56 percent. First official results are expected on Monday.

"Today's vote was a symbolic test of whether there is an anti-Socialist majority in this country. There always has been, but this time it has voted effectively," said analyst Evgenii Dainov, director of the independent Centre for Social Practices.
Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov has a secure majority in parliament -- where real power in Bulgaria lies -- but the UDF currently holds the more ceremonial post of president.

Rifts within Socialist ranks have become more public since the still unsolved October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, and whilst parliament is only half way through its four-year term, analysts said cabinet changes were a possibility.
The reform laggard of the ex-Warsaw Pact east European countries, this largely agricultural nation of just 8.4 million people has been slow to shake off its communist legacy.

An ambitious privatisation programme remains largely stalled in the face of powerful vested interests while several foreign investors privately complain Sofia still looks more to Moscow for inspiration than Brussels.
Prices are rising, the unit of currency, the lev, is falling, the central interest rate is 240 percent and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago.
